content: STX2, also referred to as Syntaxin-2 or Epimorphin, is a protein encoded by the STX2 gene in humans. This protein is a member of the syntaxin/epimorphin family, which is involved in intracellular vesicle targeting and fusion processes. Syntaxins are a large family of proteins that play a critical role in the docking and fusion of intracellular transport vesicles. The protein product of the STX2 gene is known to regulate epithelial-mesenchymal interactions, as well as epithelial cell morphogenesis and activation. Additionally, alternative splicing of the STX2 gene results in transcript variants that encode different isoforms of the protein. When the N-terminus of the protein is located on the cytosolic side of the membrane, it functions as a t-SNARE (target-SNARE) protein, facilitating intracellular vesicle docking, and is referred to as Syntaxin-2. Conversely, when the N-terminus is positioned on the extracellular surface via a non-classical secretion pathway, the protein acts as a versatile morphogen and is called Epimorphin. This membrane protein exhibits topological flexibility, allowing it to be targeted to either the apical or basolateral surface of epithelial cells in a regulated manner, depending on the specific cellular context. When expressed by mesenchymal cells, it has the ability to direct epithelial morphogenesis at the interface between epithelial and mesenchymal cells. In terms of protein-protein interactions, STX2 has been shown to interact with SNAP-25, SNAP-23, STXBP1 (Syntaxin-binding protein 1), and Syntaxin-binding protein 3. These interactions are essential for its functional roles in vesicle trafficking and cellular morphogenesis.
